channel.title: Why Did Electricity Stop Getting Cheaper?
channel.description: An interactive series by Akarsh Gopal on why electricity stopped getting cheaper, and whether it can again.

item.title: Why Did Electricity Stop Getting Cheaper?
item.description: An interactive series in nine essays: why electricity got cheaper for eighty years and then stopped, how a kilowatt-hour is made, moved and priced, and whether it can get cheaper again.

item.title: Balancing the Grid: Fifty Hertz and the Markets That Keep It
item.description: How a grid stays at fifty (or sixty) hertz second by second, how the merit order decides which plants run and lets the last plant needed set the price for all, and how markets work in time and in space, with a real day on the Texas grid.

item.title: Solar: The Engine Restarts
item.description: Why solar power got cheap when steam could not: how a photon becomes a current, the efficiency ceiling silicon has nearly reached, the factories of China and the learning curve, where the panels go in China, India, the US and Germany, yield and capacity factor, and why noon power loses its value as solar spreads.

item.title: Wind and the Fleet: Building It, Running It, and What It Is Worth
item.description: An interactive explainer of wind power and the renewable fleet: the cube law and the Betz limit, wakes, capacity factor as a design choice, interconnection queues and auctions, supply chains and the cost of capital, who carries the risk, capture rates and curtailment, hybrid plants, and the seasons of wind, sun and demand in the US, Germany, China and India.

item.title: What a Kilowatt-Hour Costs: Plants, Capital and the Bill
item.description: The costs the restarted engine does not touch: the cost of capital, first-of-a-kind nuclear, the firm capacity a clean grid needs, and the networks, taxes, levies and cross-subsidies on the bill in Germany, the United States, India and China.

item.title: Deep Dive: Transformers
item.description: An interactive explainer of power transformers: induction and flux, hysteresis and eddy-current losses, efficiency, cooling and insulation ageing, three-phase vector groups, tap changers, the family from pole-top units to generator step-ups, the 2020s supply crunch, resilience and solid-state transformers.

item.title: What a Kilowatt-Hour Is: Charge, Voltage and Heat
item.description: What is actually sold as a kilowatt-hour: charge and current, voltage as the height of an energy hill, resistance as electrons colliding with a hot lattice, and the difference between power and energy.

item.title: The Machine: Magnets, Steam and the Limits of Heat
item.description: How a spinning magnet makes electricity, why most of it still starts as heat, and the two engines of cheapening, better steam and bigger units, that ran for seventy years and then stalled.

item.title: Wires: The Network That Decides What Gets Built
item.description: An interactive explainer of the electricity network: why lines run at high voltage, how a transformer works, what limits a line, congestion and redispatch, where direct current wins, and why new lines and transformers have become the slowest part of the system to build, in China, India, the United States and Germany.

item.title: Why It Stopped, and Can It Fall Again?
item.description: The five pieces of the series put together: why electricity stopped getting cheaper in the 1970s, why its price reaches into the rest of the economy, what a megawatt-hour can become, and what would have to be true for power to get cheaper again in the US, Germany, China and India.

item.title: Deep Dive: Synthetic Fuels
item.description: An interactive explainer of electricity-based fuels: electrolysis, hydrogen, ammonia, methanol and e-kerosene; electrolyser types and efficiencies; carbon from fermenters, flue gas and the air; efficiency chains; the levelised cost of hydrogen and e-fuels; cheap hours versus utilisation; real projects and cancellations; mandates and subsidies; and where molecules make sense.

item.title: Cheaper, Then Not: A Century of Electricity Prices
item.description: Electricity in four countries, a century of US prices that fell about 5 per cent a year until 1973 and then stopped, and the question this series sets out to answer.
